source.name: Google Open Buildings 2023 (confidence 0.80 or higher), with GHSL 2020 where Open Buildings has no coverage

info.content: For the 2023 built layer, we primarily used the Google Open Buildings (2023) dataset, specifically polygons with a high confidence score (>=0.80). In areas where Google Open Buildings data were unavailable—specifically in Chad, Mali, Libya, Morocco and Western Morocco—we integrated data from the Global Human Settlement Layer from 2020. For reference, older built layers combine data from Google Open Buildings (spanning 2022 to 2021) and Google Dynamic World, specifically the "built" class.

source.name: UMD GLAD tree cover loss via Global Forest Watch

info.content: The treeloss layer shows cumulative tree cover loss from 2001 up to the selected year. It sources its data from the v1.13 University of Maryland (GLAD) tree cover loss dataset, served by Global Forest Watch. Specifically, we've focused on areas with a tree cover density exceeding 30%. Version 1.13 adds 2025 and also updates earlier years, so earlier years can look slightly different from before. Tree cover loss is not always deforestation: it includes any stand-replacing disturbance, such as fire and forestry.

source.name: NASA FIRMS active fire detections, counted in 14-day intervals per year

info.content:
For the fire layers, we utilised FIRMS data to determine the number of times a pixel burned in the year. Our methodology involved first dividing the year into 14-day intervals and then assessing if a pixel burned within each 14-day period. Finally, we summed up the number of 14-day periods a pixel experienced a fire. As a result, the maximum count for a pixel is 26 burn events within a year. The data is visualised as follows:
  • Light yellow: Pixel burned once, suggesting potential natural occurrences or management fires.
  • Orange: Pixel burned 2-3 times, possibly indicating human activity or transit.
  • Red: Pixel burned more than 3 times, hinting at agriculture, consistent human presence, or frequent transit.
  • Dark red: Pixel burned over 8 times, which may suggest industrial activities, mines, or volcanic activity.

source.name: UMD GLAD Global Cropland Expansion in the 21st Century

info.content: We sourced data from the Global Cropland Expansion in the 21st Century dataset. We are currently working to expand our layers with information from other years

source.name: UMD GLAD tree cover height 2020 via Global Forest Watch

info.content:
Estimated tree canopy height in 2020, in metres. The tiles are already coloured. Pale green is about 3 m, the middle green is about 15 m, and dark green is about 30 m. Canopy taller than 30 m stays dark green. Moving the timeline does not change this layer.
3 m15 m30 m

Source: University of Maryland GLAD dataset umd_tree_cover_height_2020, version v2022, drawn from Global Forest Watch tiles (canopy of at least 3 m). Potapov et al. 2021 describe the canopy-height model. Global Forest Watch lists 2000 and 2020 as the mapped years and links further description to the GLAD 2000–2020 land-cover dataset. Licence CC BY 4.0.

Limits: global coverage at about 30 m. North of 52°N the source calls the map a prototype. The model was calibrated on GEDI relative height at 95% and can overestimate height on slopes, including in New Zealand and Lesotho. In cities it can mix building height with tree height. Canopy below 3 m is not drawn, and heights above 30 m are not separated.
